neighboring_unit_entries.title: Mean-square zero-sum control yields finite logarithmic exceptional measure
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: A mean-square estimate for the remaining zero sum is converted into a bound for the logarithmic measure of points where that sum is too large. Applying the bound on exponentially spaced blocks and choosing the cutoff logarithmically makes the blockwise bad measures summable, which yields a total exceptional set of finite logarithmic measure. This is a substantive and reusable average-to-exceptional-set mechanism.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Both headline applications begin from a truncated explicit formula over zeta zeros, split the spectral contribution at a tunable scale, use mean-square control to suppress the difficult range, and select the scale to match the desired notion of rarity: summability of logarithmic bad-set measure in the pointwise application and a little-o averaged error in the short-interval application.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: This is a synthesis of the source's proof organization, not a claim that the two displayed calculations are identical. Because the formulas are OCR-damaged, exact cutoffs, exponents, and normalization cannot be compared from this artifact alone.
related_synthesis_entries.title: A shared truncation-and-averaging template for exceptional sets and short intervals

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Across pointwise exceptional-set, global mean-value, and short-interval results, the paper treats information about zeros as useful through controlled truncations and averaged estimates; multiplicity and pair-density information mark two distinct ways that finer zero statistics can sharpen prime-counting conclusions.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The pair-density comparison is only reported in the introduction and is not derived in this article, while the multiplicity formula is not reliably legible in OCR. The synthesis therefore remains qualitative and conditional.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Spectral truncation as a bridge from zero information to prime-counting statistics
